claim: McNemar's test for the difference between two correlated (paired) proportions uses only the discordant pairs; the statistic is (b - c)/sqrt(b + c), whose square is approximately chi-square with 1 df.

claim: Conditionally on the number of discordant pairs, b is Bin(b + c, 1/2) under H0; the exact conditional test's type I error never exceeds the nominal level.
locator: Methods, 'The McNemar exact conditional test', eq. (3)-(4)
quote: The exact conditional test is guaranteed to have type I error rates not exceeding the nominal level.
verified_how: read full text (Europe PMC XML PMC3716987)

claim: The exact conditional McNemar test is conservative: its actual type I error was barely above 3% at a 5% nominal level even with 100 pairs, which costs power and needs larger samples.
quote: The type I error rates of the McNemar exact conditional test are low and barely above 3%, even for as much as 100 matched pairs.
verified_how: read full text; scenarios N = 10..100, two-sided 5% level, complete enumeration (9595 scenarios)

claim: Mid-p = exact p minus half the point probability of the observed b; the mid-p test did not exceed the nominal level in any of 9595 scenarios, but mid-p tests are not guaranteed to stay below it.
quote: The mid-p test did not violate the nominal level in any of the 9595 scenarios considered in this article
verified_how: read full text

claim: The asymptotic McNemar test without continuity correction is the most powerful of those studied and stays close to the nominal level, with small but frequent violations; the continuity-corrected version is even more conservative than the exact test.
locator: Results, 'Type I error rates' and 'Power'; Conclusions
quote: The most powerful test is the McNemar asymptotic test (without CC), which we recommend if small but frequent violations of the nominal level is acceptable.
verified_how: read full text

claim: Fagerland et al. recommend against the exact conditional test and the continuity-corrected test in any situation.
quote: We do not recommend use of the McNemar exact conditional test nor the asymptotic test with CC in any situation.
verified_how: read full text
note: CONTRADICTION with the protocol: the thesis uses the exact conditional one-sided test. Defensible (guaranteed size <= alpha, pre-registered, power table already computed for the exact test so its conservatism is priced into n = 270), but the page should state that this source recommends mid-p instead, and that its evaluation was two-sided at 5% with N <= 100.

claim: Cohen's kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e), where p_o is observed agreement and p_e the agreement expected by chance from the two raters' marginal proportions.

claim: In Dietterich's simulations McNemar's test had low type I error, and for learning algorithms that can be run only once it was the only test with acceptable type I error.
quote: For algorithms that can be executed only once, McNemar's test is the only test with acceptable Type I error.
verified_how: read the author's preprint (Dec 1997, nc-stats.ps.gz from Dietterich's Oregon State page), abstract and Sec. 3.1 + conclusions; wording matches the journal abstract in Zotero
note: The version Dietterich used is the continuity-corrected chi-square form (|n01 - n10| - 1)^2/(n01 + n10), two-sided (preprint Sec. 3.1, p.7). He also notes it does not measure variability due to the training set; his conclusions are 'tentative' (two algorithms, three data sets).

claim: Dietterich applies McNemar's test to a 2x2 table of test-set examples misclassified by both, by only one, or by neither classifier; under H0 n01 = n10.
quote: Under the null hypothesis, the two algorithms should have the same error rate, which means that n01 = n10.
verified_how: read author preprint Sec. 3.1

claim: Holm procedure: order the p-values; compare p_(1) with alpha/m, then the next with alpha divided by the number of untested endpoints, and so on; useful for endpoints with any degree of correlation and less conservative than Bonferroni.
quote: The Holm procedure is a multi-step step-down procedure; it is useful for endpoints with any degree of correlation.
verified_how: read the FDA guidance PDF (fda.gov/media/162416)

claim: Fixed-sequence testing: test hypotheses in a pre-specified order, each at the full alpha, and stop at the first non-rejection; it needs no alpha adjustment, but after a failure later hypotheses cannot be declared significant however small their p-values.
quote: The appeal of the fixed-sequence testing method is that it does not require any alpha adjustment of the individual tests.
verified_how: read the FDA guidance PDF

claim: When success requires an effect on every one of several endpoints (co-primary endpoints) there is no multiplicity problem, but power falls (type II error rises); raising each test's alpha to compensate is not acceptable.
quote: there is no multiplicity problem when the study is designed to demonstrate efficacy on all of the separate endpoints.
verified_how: read the FDA guidance PDF

claim: The ASA's six principles: p-values can indicate incompatibility of the data with a specified model; they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or that the data were produced by chance alone; decisions should not rest only on a threshold; inference needs full reporting; a p-value does not measure effect size or importance; by itself it is not a good measure of evidence.
quote: P-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone.
